einzeiler: Why a new documentary pairing Elizabeth Holmes and Nathan Fielder is dividing critics.
kurzfassung: Film critics discuss a highly anticipated new documentary that brings together Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes and comedian Nathan Fielder. They explore Fielder's unique career of blending reality and fiction, and how the film questions the very nature of documentary storytelling. Ultimately, the project forces viewers to grapple with manipulation, deception, and whether the portrait of Holmes is sympathetic or cynical.
stichpunkte: A new documentary directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim focuses on Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes.
Despite prior coverage like podcasts and miniseries, the collaboration with Fielder makes this project uniquely unpredictable.
Fielder's past work, including Nathan For You and The Rehearsal, establishes a pattern of elaborate stunts and ethical boundary-pushing.
The documentary was sparked by Holmes inviting Fielder into her home after seeing a comedic gas station rebate episode.
The film heavily features Holmes's partner, Billy Evans, and frequently highlights her children as a form of personal framing.
Reviewers note that the movie constantly oscillates between portraying Holmes as deeply naive versus entirely cynical.
The project challenges traditional documentary tropes by actively laying bare the mechanisms of manipulation and filmmaking.
Fielder's approach is compared to Penn and Teller's style of magic, where exposing the trick becomes part of the deception itself.

clips.text: A weekly documentary columnist asserts that this particular film easily lives up to its immense hype and stands out as genuinely extraordinary.
The discussion highlights how small business owners are met with excessively elaborate and absurd solutions to their problems.
A massive production budget is used to recreate an entire bar down to the smallest background elements like deflated balloons.
A speaker reflects on how certain early comedic segments lean away from standard documentary traditions and toward aggressive prank shows.

clips.hook: Refracting back into your own navel
clips.text: Projects that ostensibly set out to examine major historical events ultimately end up serving as self-absorbed portraits of the directors themselves.

beschreibung:
The comedian Nathan Fielder came to fame as the creator and host of the Comedy Central series “Nathan for You.” The show followed Fielder as he devised outrageous schemes, ostensibly with the aim of helping various small businesses. What became clear, though, was that Fielder was less interested in helping business owners generate profits than he was in understanding the people ensnared in his plots. His next project, the HBO series “The Rehearsal,” was a similar offbeat portrait of offbeat people. At the center of both projects is Fielder himself, a documentarian whose motives can sometimes be hard to parse.
This week, Fielder’s first feature-length documentary, “You Can See Everything,” hits theaters. Co-directed by Lance Oppenheim, the movie shows Fielder embedding himself into the life of the disgraced Theranos founder and felon Elizabeth Holmes in the days leading up to her imprisonment for fraud. The film caused a big splash when it debuted at the Telluride Film Festival, in part because it presents Holmes, a mysterious and compelling cultural figure, through the eyes of Fielder, a mysterious and compelling filmmaker.
This week, the Times movie critic Alissa Wilkinson and critic at large Jason Zinoman, who covers comedy, join Michael Barbaro for a spoiler-free discussion of Nathan Fielder, his career, and why he might be the perfect person to tell the story of Elizabeth Holmes.

On Today’s Episode
Alissa Wilkinson, a movie critic at The New York Times.
Jason Zinoman, a critic at large for the Culture section of The New York Times.

Background Reading
‘The Real World’ and Nathan Fielder can both thank this cult filmmaker.
‘You Can See Everything,’ if you could only secure a ticket.
